content: A side stitch, also known as a side cramp or exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP), is a sharp, stabbing pain that occurs beneath the lower edge of the ribcage during physical activity. This pain is thought to result from the downward pulling of internal organs, such as the liver and stomach, on the diaphragm. It is more commonly experienced during activities involving repetitive vertical movements, such as running, jumping, or horseback riding. Causes The exact cause of ETAP is not fully understood, but several theories have been proposed. While one theory attributes it to the stretching of visceral ligaments due to repeated jolting and vertical motion, other possible explanations include: Diaphragmatic ischemia: Reduced blood flow to the diaphragm. Thoracic spine imbalances: Misalignments or dysfunctions in the thoracic spine. Irritation of the parietal peritoneum: This membrane lining the abdominal cavity may become irritated. The prevalence of ETAP during swimming suggests that additional factors may be involved. Side stitches most often occur on the right side of the body, likely due to the presence of the liver, the largest organ in the abdominal cavity, on that side. Some athletes also report pain in the tip of the shoulder blade, which is thought to be referred pain from the diaphragm via the phrenic nerve. Treatment To alleviate a side stitch, the following methods may be effective: 1. Stop exercising and use your fingers to press into the abdomen on the right side, just beneath the ribcage. Simultaneously, exhale deeply and forcefully through pursed lips. 2. Cease physical activity until the pain subsides. 3. Practice belly breathing: Inhale deeply while expanding your abdomen outward, and exhale while relaxing the abdominal muscles. 4. Stop exercising and bend forward to touch your toes, which may help move the liver away from the diaphragm. 5. Adjust your breathing pattern during activities like jogging (e.g., inhale for four steps and exhale for four steps). 6. Lie on your back and bring the knee on the affected side up toward your chest. Primary Prevention To reduce the likelihood of experiencing side stitches, consider the following preventive measures: Improve overall fitness levels. Strengthen the diaphragm through respiratory rehabilitation exercises. Build core strength by targeting the abdominal muscles, lower back, and obliques. Avoid consuming food or beverages two to three hours before exercising, particularly high-carbohydrate or high-osmolality drinks like reconstituted fruit juices. Stay hydrated by drinking water beforehand to prevent muscle cramps. Perform a proper warm-up before engaging in physical activity. Gradually increase the intensity of your exercise regimen. When running, synchronize your breathing with your steps: exhale when your left foot strikes the ground and inhale when your right foot strikes the ground. Opt for running on softer surfaces to minimize impact.
